title: New ROOT method charts a path to reversing biological changes once thought irreversible

beats.caption: New ROOT method charts a path to reversing biological changes once thought irreversible
Here is how scientists might reverse damaged human cells.
beats.detail: New research from KAIST explores cellular memory.
beats.narration: Here is how scientists might reverse damaged human cells, specifically those locked in abnormal states.

beats.caption: Cells usually lock into abnormal states like cancer.
beats.detail: Biology has long considered these changes irreversible.
beats.narration: Usually, cells lock into abnormal states like cancer, and biology has long considered these changes irreversible.

beats.caption: Researchers found the causal circuits controlling this lock.
beats.detail: Led by Professor Kwang-Hyun Cho at KAIST.
beats.narration: But a team at KAIST just found the causal circuits that actually control this cellular lock.

beats.caption: They call this new ROOT method of intervention.
beats.detail: It targets the core of cellular memory.
beats.narration: They call this new ROOT method, which targets the core of cellular memory to unlock the state.

beats.caption: It could restore diseased cells to normal function.
beats.detail: A major shift in how we treat cancer.
beats.narration: This could eventually restore diseased cells to normal function, marking a major shift in treating cancer.

beats.caption: This is a first step in controlled reprogramming.
beats.detail: The findings were reported via Phys.org.
beats.narration: This is a first step in controlled reprogramming, and the findings were recently reported via Phys.org.
